title: Scope, layout, schema and lint

story: Nova, our agent that turns a Jira ticket into a pull request, is writing its plan for RH-1234. It needs one fact: when it pushes to its branch, which CI workflows start? The workflow files in fcp say what runs, but not why, and the reason backend CI runs on every push while frontend CI waits for a pull request lives in a Slack thread from last spring. So Nova searches the repo and finds a page from the old team wiki, copied into a docs folder years ago, called "Every CI workflow runs on push". It was true in 2024. Nobody has touched it since, the person who wrote it has left, and nothing on the page says any of that.

A person might notice that the page looks old. An agent reads every page with the same trust, so Nova plans around a frontend CI run that will never start. A wrong page is worse than no page at all, because without the page Nova would at least have gone to read the workflow files.
hook.question: How do we write down what the team knows so that every page says who stands behind it, and a machine refuses a page that does not?

p: The code tells you what the system does. It rarely tells you why it is built that way, what was decided last year, or what breaks if you change it. Today that knowledge sits in people's heads and in Slack threads that scroll away. The R&D brain is where we write it down: a small set of short markdown pages about how our system works and why, kept in its own git repo, rnd-kb. Its tools, written in Python, live next to it in a second repo, rnd-kb-tooling.

Three kinds of readers use it. People ask it from Claude Code through a skill called kb. Nova searches it during a run with a tool called kb_search. And a Slack bot answers questions from it in public channels. You will build each of these later in this part; for now, notice what they have in common. They are all programs or people in a hurry, and none of them will stop to wonder whether a page is still true. So the brain's first job is not to be big. It is to be honest about how far each page can be trusted, which is why it starts with about 35 pages that people really ask about, not with an import of the old wiki.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what may never go in
p: Agents read the brain, and the bot repeats it in Slack, so before the first page was written, Security agreed a data scope in a file called DATA-SCOPE.md. Pages may come from the engineering and product folders in Google Drive, from Jira, from public Slack channels and from our GitHub repos. Private channels may be summarised in our own words but never quoted. Customer names, customer documents, client email, patient data (PHI, protected health information) and secrets never go in.

Customer names are the hard part, because a scanner can only block a name it knows. The list of names to block, the deny-list, is itself sensitive, so it lives in Vault and in a CI secret owned by Security, never in a repo. The lint job reads it from that secret and prints only the file and line of a match, never the matched word.

read.h: A page says who stands behind it
p: Every brain page starts with a small block of YAML between two --- lines, called frontmatter. You may know it from blog engines and docs sites; here it carries the page's trust label. The body below it is normal markdown for people and agents to read. This is the page Nova needed, written the brain's way.

Four fields do the work. owner names a person or a GitHub team who answers for the page. reviewed is the date that owner last checked the page against the code, and review_every says how long that check stays good. confidence says how sure the owner is, and sources lists where every fact can be checked. Put the old wiki page next to this one and the difference is clear: the wiki page could not fill in a single one of these fields honestly.

code.text:
---
title: Which CI workflow runs what, and when
owner: "@RhinoHealth/devops"
reviewed: 2026-10-05
review_every: 90d
confidence: high
sources:
  - https://github.com/RhinoHealth/fcp/tree/main/.github/workflows
applies_to:
  - "fcp:.github/workflows/**"
---
# Which CI workflow runs what, and when

Cloud, client and sdk CI run on every push, to any branch.
Frontend CI runs on pull requests, so a push alone starts nothing.

notes.text: A GitHub team or a person's login. It must be listed in OWNERS.yml, which also says where to reach that owner in Slack.
The day a person last checked this page against the code, not the day someone fixed a typo.
high: checked against main recently. med: mostly checked. low: an AI draft nobody has checked yet.
At least one place a reader can check the facts: a link to code, a PR, a doc, or a Jira key.
repo:glob, the code this page describes. Later tools use it to warn the owner when that code changes.

p: Many tools read this frontmatter: the lint, the search, a weekly reminder to owners and the Slack bot. If each tool parsed it in its own way, they would soon disagree about what a page is. So the shape of a page is written once, as a Pydantic model in rnd-kb-tooling, and every tool imports it. Pydantic is to Python what zod is to TypeScript: you declare fields with types and rules, and Page.model_validate(data) either gives you a Page or raises a ValidationError that lists every field that is wrong.

Two settings matter more than they look. extra="forbid" turns an unknown key into an error, so a typo such as confidense cannot pass unnoticed as an unused extra field. And confidence has no default, so a page that forgets to say how sure it is fails instead of quietly counting as high. The model also knows how trust fades: due() is the date of the next review, and effective_confidence() reads a page as low once it is more than twice overdue, without anyone editing the file.

code.text:
from datetime import date, timedelta
from typing import Annotated, Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

Source = Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r"^(RH-\d+|https://\S+)$")]
RepoGlob = Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r"^(fcp|infrastructure|gitops|byte):\S+$")]
DAYS = {"30d": 30, "90d": 90, "180d": 180, "365d": 365}


class Page(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")

    title: str = Field(min_length=8, max_length=100)
    owner: str = Field(pattern=r"^@[\w.-]+(/[\w.-]+)?$")
    reviewed: date
    review_every: Literal["30d", "90d", "180d", "365d"] = "90d"
    confidence: Literal["high", "med", "low"]
    sources: list[Source] = Field(min_length=1)
    applies_to: list[RepoGlob] = []

    def due(self) -> date:
        return self.reviewed + timedelta(days=DAYS[self.review_every])

    def effective_confidence(self, today: date) -> str:
        too_old = (today - self.reviewed).days > 2 * DAYS[self.review_every]
        return "low" if too_old else self.confidence

notes.text: Annotated attaches a rule to a plain str: a source is a Jira key like RH-6812 or an https link, nothing else.
Pages live outside fcp, so applies_to must name the repo before the glob.
Unknown keys are errors. This is what catches a misspelled field name.
No default value: every page has to say how sure it is.
min_length=1: a page with no source cannot be checked, so it cannot be merged.
More than twice overdue reads as low everywhere: in search, in the index and in the bot.

read.h: Lint checks what a schema cannot see
p: A schema checks the shape of one page on its own. Some mistakes only show up when you look outside the page. The old wiki page has a perfectly valid owner string, @old-wiki-bot, but nobody by that name is in OWNERS.yml. A page can link to another page that was renamed, or claim to describe fcp:client/old_folder/** after that folder was deleted. kb lint is the command that runs the schema on every page and then makes these outside checks.

It prints one line per problem in the form path:line: message, the same shape a compiler uses, so a person can click it and an agent can act on it. It exits with 1 when there is any problem, which is what makes it useful as a required check on every pull request in rnd-kb. One thing is deliberately only a warning: a review that is overdue. An overdue page does not block an unrelated pull request, because its trust is already lowered by effective_confidence(), and the owner gets a reminder instead.

notes.text: The schema first. Its errors already say which field is wrong, so we print them as they are.
Valid shape is not enough: the owner must be someone we can actually reach.
A relative link to another page must point at a file that exists.
CI checks out fcp next to the brain, so each applies_to glob must match at least one real file.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the lint as a required check
p: In CI the lint runs from a reusable workflow in rnd-kb-tooling (a workflow other repos call with workflow_call, as in the lesson on reusable workflows). rnd-kb calls it on every pull request, pinned by commit SHA, so a change to the tooling cannot change rnd-kb's check without a pull request in rnd-kb.

The job runs gitleaks, a secret scanner, first, before any other repo is checked out, so it scans only the brain's own files. Then it takes a short-lived token from a small GitHub App with read access, checks out rnd-kb-tooling and fcp (fcp is needed to test the applies_to globs), and runs kb lint and kb scan, which looks for patient-like data and deny-list terms. The repo's ruleset lists the job as a required check, so no page merges with a red lint.

lab.title: A schema and a lint for brain pages
lab.goal: Validate brain pages against one Pydantic model, then extend the lint so it also refuses an owner nobody can reach.

guess.q: A page's frontmatter says confidense: low (a typo) and the Page model has extra="forbid" and no default for confidence. What does Page.model_validate do with it?

options.text: It accepts the page and ignores the unknown key, so the page has no confidence.
options.why: That is what extra="ignore" would do, and a missing confidence would still be an error because the field has no default.

options.text: It raises a ValidationError with two problems: confidence is missing, and confidense is not allowed.
options.why: forbid turns the unknown key into an error, and the required field is reported missing. You see both lines in the first lint run.

options.text: It fixes the typo and reads the page as low.
options.why: Pydantic never guesses what you meant. It reports what is wrong and leaves the fix to the author.

follow.say: Write the lint. For now it only runs the schema on every page; the outside checks are your Build step.
follow.do:
cat > lint.py <<'EOF'
import re
import sys
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import yaml
from pydantic import ValidationError

from schema import Page

FRONTMATTER = re.compile(r"\A---\n(.*?)\n---\n", re.DOTALL)


def lint_page(path: Path, owners: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    match = FRONTMATTER.match(path.read_text())
    if not match:
        return [f"{path}:1: missing frontmatter"]
    try:
        page = Page.model_validate(yaml.safe_load(match.group(1)))
    except ValidationError as err:
        return [f"{path}:1: {'.'.join(map(str, e['loc']))}: {e['msg']}" for e in err.errors()]
    problems = []
    # Build it: check the owner and the reviewed date here
    return problems


def main() -> None:
    kb = Path(sys.argv[1])
    owners = set(yaml.safe_load((kb / "OWNERS.yml").read_text()))
    problems = [p for f in sorted(kb.rglob("*.md")) for p in lint_page(f, owners)]
    for problem in problems:
        print(problem)
    print(f"kb lint: {len(problems)} problems")
    sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
EOF

explain: Why does the brain need an owner and sources on every page, when a normal wiki works without them?
Why is the shape of a page written once as a Pydantic model instead of being checked separately by each tool?
Why is an unknown owner an error but an overdue review only a warning?
lab.done: Your lint catches all three bad pages, warns about the overdue one without failing, and exits with 0 once the author fixes are in.

check.q: An author writes confidense: high by mistake. The Page model uses extra="forbid" and confidence has no default. What does kb lint print?

options.text: Nothing: the page passes, because unknown keys are ignored
options.why: That would be extra="ignore". With forbid, an unknown key is an error.

options.text: Two lines for that page: confidence is missing, and confidense is not permitted
options.why: The typo is an extra key, and the real field is required, so the schema reports both and lint exits with 1.

options.text: A warning only, because the page is still readable
options.why: Only an overdue review is a warning. Bad frontmatter always fails, because every tool depends on it.

check.q: A page says confidence: high, review_every: 90d, and was reviewed 200 days ago. What confidence does the Slack bot show?

options.text: high, because that is what the file says
options.why: The file is not edited, but every tool asks effective_confidence(), and 200 days is more than twice 90.

options.text: med, halfway between the file and the age
options.why: There is no halfway value in the model: a page reads as its own confidence or as low.

options.text: low, because the page is more than twice overdue
options.why: effective_confidence() returns low after 2 × 90 = 180 days, so search, the index and the bot all treat the page as a hint to check, not a fact, until its owner reviews it.

check.q: Why is the page shape a Pydantic model that lint, search, the reminders and the bot all import, instead of a description in a README?

options.text: So every tool agrees on what a page is, including rules like when a page reads as low
options.why: Written once in code, the rule cannot drift. If the bot and the search computed trust differently, an agent and a person could see different confidence for the same page.

options.text: Because Python cannot read YAML without Pydantic
options.why: pyyaml reads YAML on its own. Pydantic adds the rules: types, patterns, required fields and the methods.

options.text: Because a model makes pages load faster
options.why: Speed is not the point. Agreement between tools is.

p: The brain lives in two repos. RhinoHealth/rnd-kb holds the pages in engineering/, product/, decisions/ (ADR-NNNN-<slug>.md) and runbooks/, plus templates/page.md, OWNERS.yml, README.md and DATA-SCOPE.md at the root; index.md and index.json are generated by kb index and never edited by hand. RhinoHealth/rnd-kb-tooling is a uv project on Python 3.13 (black and isort at 120, pre-commit, like fcp) with the kb_tools package and a kb console script. The plan first put the pages in a kb/ folder inside fcp; they moved to their own repos, fcp keeps only a one-line pointer in its root CLAUDE.md, and the choice is recorded as decisions/ADR-0001-brain-home.md.

kb lint prints path:line: message, and kb index writes index.md and index.json for search, the PR comments, ingest and the bot. On every rnd-kb pull request a thin caller runs rnd-kb-tooling's reusable kb-lint.yml, pinned by SHA with secrets: inherit: gitleaks first, then a rhino-kb GitHub App token (contents:read on rnd-kb, rnd-kb-tooling and fcp), kb lint with --repo fcp=.repos/fcp --index-check, and kb scan with KB_DENY_TERMS from a Security-owned secret. DevOps adds kb-lint / lint as a required check to rnd-kb's ruleset, which is fcp's ruleset pattern: a PR, exactly one approval, stale approvals dismissed, no bypass for agent apps.

tickets.why: The data scope in DATA-SCOPE.md, where the deny-list lives, and the decision that the brain lives in rnd-kb and rnd-kb-tooling (ADR-0001).
The folders, OWNERS.yml, the page template and the Page model in schema.py.
kb lint with its outside checks, kb index, the pytest fixtures and the pre-commit hook.
The reusable kb-lint workflow with gitleaks, the rhino-kb App, kb scan, and the required check.

words.plain: A small git repo of owned, sourced pages about how our system works and why, read by people, Nova and a Slack bot.
The YAML block between two --- lines at the top of a markdown page; for the brain it is the page's trust label.
A Python class that declares fields with types and rules and validates data against them, like a zod schema.
The command that validates every page and checks owners, dates, links and paths, printing path:line: message per problem.
The confidence a reader should see today: the page's own value, or low once the page is more than twice overdue.

review.q: Name the four frontmatter fields that make a page trustworthy and what each one answers.
review.a: owner: who answers for it. reviewed (with review_every): when it was last checked and for how long that holds. confidence: how sure the owner is. sources: where each fact can be checked.

review.q: Your lint is green but a page's owner left the company last month. Which check should have caught it, and what has to change for it to fire?
review.a: The owner check against OWNERS.yml. The person must be removed from OWNERS.yml, and then lint fails for every page they own until a new owner is set.

review.q: Why does extra="forbid" matter more for a brain page than for most data?
review.a: A misspelled field such as confidense would otherwise be ignored, and with a default value the page could read as more trusted than its author meant. Agents read that value as fact.

remember: Every brain page carries its own trust label (owner, review date, confidence, sources), and one schema in code plus a lint refuse any page that cannot fill it in honestly.
